html:
The Zo'é are a small people of the forest between the Cuminapanema and Erepecuru rivers in northern Pará, Brazil. They speak a language of the Tupi-Guarani branch of the Tupian family. They are known for the poturu, a long wooden plug worn in the lower lip from childhood.

They lived without lasting contact with outsiders until 1987, when an evangelical mission settled near them. Disease then killed many. In 1991 Brazil's Indigenous agency, FUNAI, took over, removed the mission and limited outside access to protect their health. About 300 Zo'é live today on their own demarcated land. Neighbours to the north include the Wayana and Aparai.
